title: cold-start-warmup-profiles-quantized-inference-overheads-march2026
summary: Short experimental note describing cold-start and warmup behavior for quantized model variants (INT8/GPTQ/AWQ/FP8) across kernel implementations. Focus is on observable latency/throughput overheads immediately after model activation, energy/thermal observations in multi-tenant pods, and pragmatic mitigations for meeting latency SLOs.
objectives: Measure and explain the additional latency and throughput penalties that occur during model cold-start and early-warmup for quantized variants compared to FP16 baseline. Produce actionable mitigations for reducing first-byte/first-token and tail latency impact in hosted and Dedicated settings.
experimental-setup: Cluster: 4x A100-40GB nodes (k8s pod per test), Ubuntu 20.04, CUDA 11.8, cuBLAS/cudnn versions pinned. Serving runtime: redwood-serving v2.14. Bench harness: bench/warmup_profile.py (local script). Models tested: llama-2-13b-hf (hf weights converted), bloomed-7b1 (for small-model comparison). Quant methods: native FP16 (baseline), GPTQ-INT8, AWQ-INT8, FP8-mixed (experimental kernels). Kernels: fused-gemm-v1, matmul-tiling-v2, cuBLAS-fastpath. Each run repeated 6x; node reboot between major config changes. Warmup pattern: idle period 300s, then single inference request of a 16-token prompt, followed by sustained streaming generation to 512 tokens. All measurements captured with perf metrics + NVML for power and nsys traces for the first request. Note: to reduce noise we pinned tests to single-socket GPU and isolated other pods.
workloads: A) short interactive prompt (16 token request) B) chat-style prefix (128 tokens) followed by streaming generation to 512 tokens C) synthetic micro-bench warmup (repeated 8-token queries x 10) used for kernel auto-tune triggering.
metrics_collected: first_byte_latency_ms, first_token_latency_ms, steady_state_p95_ms, throughput_tok_s, gpu_memory_alloc_time_ms, kv_cache_alloc_time_ms, kernel_jit_time_ms, nvml_power_w, observed_gpu_temp_c, compile/cache_hits
raw_results_summary: 1) FP16 baseline: first-token latency median 55ms; steady-state p95 18-22ms. 2) GPTQ-INT8: cold first-token median 78ms (+42% vs FP16), steady-state p95 20-24ms. 3) AWQ-INT8: cold first-token median 65ms (+18%), steady-state p95 19-22ms. 4) FP8-mixed: cold first-token median 92ms (+67%), steady-state p95 17-21ms. 5) Kernel choice matters: fused-gemm-v1 reduced first-token kernel_jit_time by ~35ms vs matmul-tiling-v2 on INT8 variants. 6) GPU memory allocation and KV cache zeroing accounted for ~10-30ms of cold overhead depending on model size and allocator behavior. 7) NVML power traces: quantized variants showed 10-15% lower steady-state wattage but similar peak watts during first 1-2 bursts.
key_findings: - Cold-start overhead is dominated by three things: (A) lazy kernel heuristics / JIT/autotune (kernel_jit_time), (B) large contiguous GPU memory allocations for quantized weight layouts and KV caches (gpu_memory_alloc_time), (C) temperature-related scheduler slowdown when device was previously saturated (observed in multi-tenant pod tests).
detailed-observations: 1) Kernel JIT/autotune: On A100 with our runtime, some quant kernels fallback to a tuning path which probes multiple cuBLAS/cuDNN algorithms on the first executions; this added 25-45ms depending on kernel. Fused kernels we control avoid this by shipping pre-selected kernel-code-paths. 2) Memory allocation: our allocator was doing large cudaMalloc+memset sequences for quant layouts; using persistent pooled allocators reduced allocation time from ~28ms to ~6ms for 13B models. 3) KV cache zeroing: zeroing large KV buffers after allocation added noticeable overhead; switching to lazily-initialized zero-on-demand reduced first-token penalty by ~8-12ms. 4) FP8 path: FP8 conversion/packing step happens on load if weights were stored in FP16; conversion cost contributed ~30-40ms to cold startup for 13B unless weights persisted in quantized format on disk. 5) Multi-tenant thermal effect: on nodes with sustained 90% utilization prior to idle, the first-burst throughput dropped 8-12% and kernel runtimes were slightly higher; likely due to GPU clock governors and temperature scaling. 6) AWQ vs GPTQ: AWQ's weight layout tends to be more kernel-friendly for our fused-gemm implementation, hence lower kernel_jit_time and slightly lower first-token latencies.
recommendations: 1) Pre-warm strategy: maintain a thin hot-pool of pre-initialized model processes per SKU and quant profile; pre-warm involves allocating weight buffers, one short synthetic prompt to trigger kernel selection, and KV cache allocation. 2) Persistent quantized artifacts: persist AWQ/GPTQ quantized weight files and avoid on-load conversion where possible. 3) Allocator changes: adopt pooled/pinned allocator to avoid repeated cudaMalloc memsets. 4) Lazy KV zeroing: defer zeroing until first need or use on-demand read path. 5) Kernel shipping: for hosted tiers, ship pre-baked fused kernels for common quant formats to avoid autotune probe. 6) Scheduling: avoid co-locating cold-start heavy workloads with prior-saturated GPU tenants; use soft placement hints in Dedicated pools. 7) SLO adjustments: add a short warmup SLA window (e.g., 200ms buffer for first-token on model scale-up) and track cold-start rate per route.
action_items: - (Ethan) prototype persistent pooled allocator and measure allocation-time reduction (owner: Ethan Ruiz). - (Lina) add hot-pool prototype to dedicated autoscaler and measure cost impact vs latency reduction. - (Owen) create synthetic warmup endpoint and instrumentation for kernel_jit_time telemetry. - (Maya) update docs and add recommended pre-warm commands to onboarding playbook.
cost-note: Maintaining a hot-pool increases steady spend; rough back-of-envelope: 1 pre-warmed 13B AWQ process per 1000 qps reduces first-token violations by ~70% at ~4-6% added infra cost (based on our Dedicated pricing model). Exact numbers depend on GPU type and occupancy.
practical-playbook-snippets:
Commands used for measurement:
- python bench/warmup_profile.py --model llama-2-13b-hf --quant gptq --kernel fused-gemm-v1 --prompt 'Hello' --stream --repeat 6
- nv-nsight profile --session first_request.nsys --target-process <pid>
Allocator toggles were controlled via env: RW_ALLOC_MODE=pooled|default. Persistent quant load: python convert_and_save_quant.py --method awq --out-path /mnt/quant-cache/llama2-13b-awq.bin
Deploy hot-pool example (k8s): k apply -f hotpool-llama13b-awq.yaml
caveats-and-open-questions: - We saw variance across firmware and driver versions; further runs needed across Ampere/Blackwell families. - How much of the kernel_jit_time can be eliminated by shipping precomputed heuristics for cuBLAS/cuDNN vs implementing our own fused kernels? - Need cost/benefit analysis for Dedicated customers who may prefer reserved always-on instances vs hot-pool. - FP8 path is experimental; additional verification for numerical parity required before recommending as general default.
next_steps: 1) Run the same warmup profile on T4 and H100 testbeds (owner: Ethan) 2) Prototype pooled allocator + lazy-kv and report delta (owner: Ethan) 3) Implement hot-pool machinery in autoscaler and run A/B on 3 customer routes (owner: Lina) 4) Draft proposed SLO wording for cold-start buffer and present at eng-runtime sync (owner: Maya).
raw_notes:
Observational notes captured while running traces:
- On an 13B AWQ run the first cuBLAS call selected algorithm 7 after probing; probing lasted ~28ms. With fused-gemm prebound the call path used algorithm 3 and time dropped.
- FP8 load: conversion from stored fp16 -> fp8 in-place burned ~34ms and used additional host CPU cycles; consider doing conversion offline.
- On one node with noisy neighbor we saw temp spike to 78C and clocks lowered, saw 9% higher p95 for first 50 tokens.
- When running 2x quantized models concurrently the allocator fragmentation increased allocation times by ~40% compared to single tenant.
- Quick test: enabling CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING did not change cold-start numbers meaning the bottleneck is not async kernel launch ordering but allocation/jit/convert work.
references: Other internal artifacts: quant-kernel-impact-playbook-nov2024, kernel-sampling-smokehouse-int8-fp8-gptq-awq-jun2026. External refs: paper 'Reducing Startup Latency in GPU Inference' (arXiv 2025), cuBLAS docs on algorithm selection.
conclusion: Cold-start and warmup overhead for quantized variants is real but addressable. The largest wins are implementation-level (allocator+lazy-kv + shipping fused kernels) and operational (hot-pool / pre-warm). For immediate SLO protection we recommend a short warmup buffer combined with a small hot-pool for high-value SKUs while we iterate on kernel shipping and allocator improvements.
